With this network-level overview in place, the following section introduces the significant proteins in greater detail and considers how their annotated functions may relate to stroke-associated mechanisms. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
Among the proteins listed, BSG stands out as the most directly relevant to stroke pathobiology because several of its established functions converge on mechanisms that are central to ischemic and hemorrhagic brain injury, namely axonal integrity, neuronal survival, myelin maintenance, and limitation of regenerative sprouting. Stroke commonly produces secondary white-matter injury, axonal degeneration, and progressive neuronal loss beyond the initial vascular insult. In this context, the observation that BSG is required for maintenance of normal axon myelination and for prevention of degeneration of myelinated axons in adults suggests a plausible role in determining tissue resilience and long-term neurological outcome after stroke. Its reported anti-apoptotic effect on motoneurons further strengthens its relevance, because apoptosis contributes substantially to delayed neuronal injury in peri-infarct regions. At the same time, BSG also functions as a negative regulator of neurite outgrowth, acting through RTN4R, RTN4RL2, and ganglioside-dependent pathways. This inhibitory activity is particularly important for stroke because functional recovery depends in part on axonal sprouting and circuit remodeling in surviving tissue. Therefore, BSG may have a dual role in stroke: it may be beneficial in preserving myelinated axons and neuronal survival during injury, yet detrimental during recovery by restricting neurite extension and axonal regeneration. This combination of neuroprotective and regeneration-limiting properties makes BSG especially noteworthy as a candidate modulator of both acute injury progression and post-stroke repair.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

In contrast to BSG, which appears more closely tied to neuronal and axonal biology, TNF may be relevant to stroke primarily through immunological mechanisms rather than through direct antimicrobial functions. Although the antimicrobial activities against bacteria and Candida albicans are biologically interesting, the more stroke-relevant feature in the present annotation is its ability to bind CCR6 and drive chemotaxis of immune cell populations, including immature dendritic cells and memory T cells. Post-stroke pathology is strongly shaped by neuroinflammation and peripheral immune-cell recruitment, both of which influence infarct evolution, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, secondary tissue injury, and later repair processes. A protein that recruits CCR6-expressing leukocytes could therefore contribute to inflammatory cell trafficking in the post-stroke setting, potentially modulating the balance between detrimental inflammation and adaptive immune responses. In addition, the antimicrobial properties may have indirect clinical relevance because stroke patients are highly susceptible to secondary infections, including pneumonia and other opportunistic infections, which substantially worsen outcomes. Thus, while TNF is less directly tied than BSG to neuronal and axonal mechanisms of stroke injury, its chemotactic activity through CCR6 makes it notable as a plausible mediator of immune responses that are increasingly recognized as important determinants of stroke severity and recovery.[PubMed:10837369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10837369) [PubMed:9202117](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9202117) [PubMed:30050988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30050988) [PubMed:10521347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10521347) [PubMed:20068036](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20068036)

### extracellular matrix structural constituent (GO:0005201) 

The pathway termed extracellular matrix structural constituent refers to the molecular function of proteins and proteoglycans that physically build, stabilize, and organize the extracellular matrix, thereby preserving tissue architecture and mechanical integrity. In the brain and vasculature, these structural constituents include basement membrane components such as collagen type four, laminin, and fibronectin, as well as perineuronal net components and other matrix-associated proteoglycans that surround neurons, glial cells, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. These molecules are not merely passive scaffolds; rather, they define the structural framework of the neurovascular environment, regulate adhesion between cells and matrix, maintain blood-brain barrier integrity, shape vessel wall stiffness, and constrain or permit synaptic and cellular plasticity. In cerebrovascular disease, the extracellular matrix is especially important because stroke develops and evolves within tissues whose survival depends on intact vascular walls, stable basement membranes, and preserved interactions among endothelial cells, pericytes, astroglia, neurons, and matrix adhesion zones. The cited literature shows that structural extracellular matrix constituents are altered across several stroke-relevant settings: thromboembolic risk states such as atrial fibrillation involve fibroelastic infiltration of the extracellular matrix and wall remodeling that favor thrombogenesis; cerebral small vessel disease is strongly linked to extracellular matrix genes, particularly type four collagens; ischemic stroke induces region- and time-dependent accumulation or redistribution of collagen type four and fibronectin in the neurovascular matrix; perineuronal nets composed of extracellular matrix structural molecules are degraded and remodeled after focal cerebral ischemia; and vascular stiffness preceding stroke susceptibility is associated with transcriptional changes in extracellular matrix structural constituents. Collectively, this pathway represents the structural backbone of both cerebral vessels and neural microenvironments, and its disruption can influence stroke risk, acute tissue injury, blood-brain barrier failure, hemorrhagic vulnerability, inflammation, thrombosis, and post-stroke repair.

Building on this structural overview, the relationship between extracellular matrix structural constituents and stroke appears multifaceted, spanning stroke predisposition, acute ischemic damage, hemorrhagic vessel fragility, and recovery-associated plasticity. At the level of stroke risk, remodeling of structural extracellular matrix within the atrial wall contributes to thrombogenic conditions in atrial fibrillation, including fibroelastic infiltration and endocardial injury, thereby promoting cardioembolic stroke formation according to the framework of disturbed flow, vessel wall abnormality, and altered blood constituents described in the review of thrombogenesis in atrial fibrillation (PubMed:19135613). In the cerebral vasculature, extracellular matrix structural proteins are central to small vessel integrity; genetic studies identify type four collagens and other extracellular matrix-related mechanisms as major determinants of cerebral small vessel disease, linking matrix defects to ischemic stroke and dementia, while abnormal deposition of collagen type four and aggrecan in hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy illustrates how excess or disordered matrix can weaken vessel walls and predispose to hemorrhagic stroke (PubMed:25899296, PubMed:23973860). During acute ischemic stroke, the extracellular matrix of the neurovascular unit is rapidly remodeled: experimental and human studies show increased immunosignals of collagen type four and fibronectin in ischemic regions, with collagen type four remaining vessel-associated and fibronectin spreading into the parenchyma, indicating profound alteration of the neurovascular matrix adhesion zone alongside blood-brain barrier disruption (PubMed:33192578). Complementary transcriptional work demonstrates that ischemia broadly perturbs expression of neurovascular and extracellular matrix components, emphasizing that matrix structural change is an early and coordinated part of infarct evolution rather than a secondary bystander phenomenon (PubMed:31089963). Reviews of stroke pathophysiology further place extracellular matrix remodeling downstream of metabolic failure, inflammation, and matrix metalloproteinase activity, highlighting its contribution to blood-brain barrier permeability, leukocyte infiltration, and chronic maladaptive tissue organization (PubMed:33066304, PubMed:35394716, PubMed:36119117). In neural tissue itself, extracellular matrix structural constituents that form perineuronal nets are highly sensitive to ischemia: focal cerebral ischemia causes loss of aggrecan, neurocan, versican, and related net structures around inhibitory neurons, while later transient loosening and remodeling of these nets precede motor recovery, suggesting that controlled modification of structural matrix can both reflect injury severity and enable post-stroke plasticity (PubMed:28860977, PubMed:37658339). Finally, biomaterial studies using brain-derived extracellular matrix show that region-specific matrix scaffolds can promote neural survival and recovery under stroke-mimetic conditions, supporting the concept that restoring appropriate structural and biochemical matrix cues may be therapeutically beneficial after stroke (PubMed:40195414). Taken together, the available evidence suggests that extracellular matrix structural constituents are integral to the initiation of stroke through vascular and thrombotic mechanisms, to the propagation of injury through blood-brain barrier and neurovascular matrix disruption, and to the subsequent balance between scarring and repair through regulation of neuronal and vascular remodeling.[PubMed:19135613](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19135613) [PubMed:25899296](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25899296) [PubMed:23973860](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23973860) [PubMed:33192578](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33192578) [PubMed:31089963](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31089963) [PubMed:33066304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33066304) [PubMed:35394716](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35394716) [PubMed:36119117](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36119117) [PubMed:28860977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28860977) [PubMed:37658339](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37658339) [PubMed:40195414](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40195414) 

Consistent with this literature-based context, there were 14 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway termed extracellular matrix structural constituent. This enrichment indicates that a defined set of 14 proteins converges on a molecular function that is directly relevant to the structural organization of the neurovascular extracellular matrix, including basement membrane architecture, vascular wall stability, blood-brain barrier preservation, and matrix-dependent cellular interactions that are central to stroke susceptibility, acute tissue injury, and post-injury remodeling. In the context of stroke, the concentration of 14 proteins within this functionally coherent pathway supports the interpretation that extracellular matrix structural biology represents a quantitatively important component of disease-associated molecular alteration, particularly because the extracellular matrix governs tissue mechanics, endothelial support, neuronal microenvironment stability, and the balance between injury propagation and repair after cerebrovascular insult. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 14 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=77F1247DCBD04E54).

![PPI Network](imgs/a3bccdf4-f858-41d9-8b35-b0c83f0eddbd.png)

To further contextualize this enrichment result, the significant proteins identified in the analysis are introduced below in greater detail. TNC stands out as one of the most stroke-relevant proteins in this list because its annotated functions align closely with central processes in ischemic brain injury and recovery. Stroke induces extensive extracellular matrix remodeling, neuroinflammation, axonal damage, and a subsequent attempt at tissue repair. As an extracellular matrix glycoprotein involved in neuronal migration, axon guidance, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal regeneration, TNC is highly relevant to post-stroke neural remodeling. Its ability to promote neurite outgrowth suggests a potential role in regenerative responses after ischemic injury, when surviving neurons attempt to re-establish connectivity. In parallel, its integrin-binding properties and pro-angiogenic activity indicate a plausible contribution to vascular remodeling, endothelial sprouting, and neurovascular unit repair after stroke. These same matrix-remodeling and angiogenic functions may also have pathogenic significance, because excessive extracellular matrix activation can amplify inflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. Thus, TNC is important because it sits at the interface of injury and repair, linking extracellular matrix signaling, neuronal plasticity, and angiogenesis, which are three core mechanisms in stroke pathobiology.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

In a related but somewhat more inflammation-centered manner, CHI3L1 is highly relevant to stroke because its functional profile strongly implicates it in inflammation, tissue remodeling, macrophage polarization, and cellular stress responses, all of which are major determinants of stroke severity and recovery. Following cerebral ischemia, innate immune activation and remodeling of injured tissue shape both acute damage and later repair. CHI3L1 is particularly notable because it is linked to inflammatory regulation, M2 macrophage differentiation, apoptosis control, and adaptation to tissue injury. These properties suggest that it could influence the balance between detrimental neuroinflammation and reparative immune responses after stroke. Its association with AKT1 signaling and IL8 production further supports a role in cytokine-driven injury cascades and leukocyte recruitment, processes that contribute to blood-brain barrier disruption and secondary damage. At the same time, its roles in host tolerance and tissue protection indicate that CHI3L1 may also participate in endogenous repair programs. Therefore, CHI3L1 is an important candidate in stroke biology because it connects post-ischemic inflammation with remodeling and survival pathways, making it potentially relevant as both a biomarker and a mediator of outcome.

Shifting from inflammatory remodeling to vascular signaling, IGFBP7 is particularly interesting in the context of stroke because its functions converge on vascular biology, endothelial signaling, and angiogenesis. Cerebrovascular integrity and post-ischemic vascular remodeling are central to stroke pathogenesis and recovery. The ability of IGFBP7 to stimulate prostacyclin production is noteworthy, as prostacyclin is a vasoprotective mediator with anti-platelet, vasodilatory, and endothelial-supportive effects, all of which are highly relevant to cerebral ischemia and microvascular perfusion. Its role in cell adhesion and its recently described function as a CD93 ligand involved in angiogenesis further suggest participation in endothelial repair and neovascular responses after stroke. Because angiogenesis can support tissue recovery in the subacute phase, while dysregulated vascular signaling can also contribute to edema or abnormal permeability, IGFBP7 may influence multiple phases of stroke evolution. Overall, IGFBP7 stands out as a plausible modulator of neurovascular unit function and post-stroke vascular remodeling.[PubMed:38218180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38218180) 

Alongside these vascular effects, EFEMP1 appears relevant to stroke primarily because of its potential effects on EGFR signaling, cell migration, adhesion, and glial biology. EGFR-dependent pathways are implicated in cellular survival, reactive gliosis, vascular responses, and tissue remodeling after brain injury. By binding EGFR and inducing receptor autophosphorylation, EFEMP1 may modulate signaling networks that influence how neural and vascular cells respond to ischemic stress. Its additional roles in cell adhesion and migration suggest possible involvement in extracellular matrix reorganization and reparative cellular movement after stroke. The annotation that EFEMP1 may regulate glial cell migration and differentiation, as well as support neurite outgrowth indirectly through glial cells, is especially notable because glia are central regulators of post-stroke inflammation, scar formation, and neuronal recovery. Although the direct stroke connection is less explicit than for TNC or CHI3L1, EFEMP1 has a functionally credible link to neurovascular remodeling and regenerative responses after ischemic injury.

Extending this theme of repair-related biology, SPON1 is notable for stroke because it combines neuronal adhesion and neurite outgrowth functions with a likely role in vascular smooth muscle biology. Recovery after stroke depends in part on axonal sprouting, circuit rewiring, and restoration of neurovascular integrity. A protein that promotes neuronal attachment and neurite extension may contribute to regenerative plasticity in peri-infarct tissue. In addition, the reference to vascular smooth muscle cell relevance suggests a possible role in vessel wall biology, which is important not only for cerebrovascular stability but also for remodeling after ischemic injury. These dual neural and vascular properties make SPON1 conceptually important in stroke, where both neuronal network repair and vascular adaptation are required for functional recovery. Although the supplied annotation does not include direct stroke-specific evidence, its biology is consistent with mechanisms of post-stroke repair.

By comparison, CD4 is less directly connected to stroke than several extracellular matrix and vascular proteins in this list, but it remains relevant because it is a central immune marker and mediator of adaptive immunity. Stroke triggers profound immune alterations, including systemic immunosuppression and shifts in T-cell responses that can affect both brain injury and susceptibility to post-stroke infection. CD4-positive T cells have established roles in neuroinflammation, and dysregulated T-cell activation can contribute to secondary injury after cerebral ischemia. The annotation provided here emphasizes microbial receptor functions rather than immunoregulation per se; however, these infection-related roles still have indirect relevance because infectious burden and immune dysfunction can modify stroke risk and outcomes. In particular, HIV infection is associated with elevated cerebrovascular risk through chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and coagulopathy, making CD4 biologically relevant in specific stroke-associated clinical contexts.[PubMed:12089508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089508) [PubMed:16331979](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16331979) [PubMed:2214026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2214026) [PubMed:9641677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9641677) [PubMed:17346169](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17346169) [PubMed:7909607](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7909607) 

Returning to more structural extracellular matrix considerations, LTBP2 is potentially relevant to stroke because elastic fiber organization is fundamental to vascular wall integrity and biomechanics. Cerebral vessels require properly assembled extracellular matrix and elastic components to maintain compliance and resist injury. A protein involved in elastic-fiber architecture could therefore influence susceptibility to vascular fragility, abnormal remodeling, or small-vessel dysfunction, all of which are pertinent to stroke pathogenesis, particularly hemorrhagic stroke and chronic cerebrovascular disease. Although the supplied annotation is limited and does not directly mention brain or vascular signaling, the structural extracellular matrix role of LTBP2 makes it a plausible contributor to cerebrovascular stability. Its relevance is therefore mechanistically credible but currently less specific than proteins linked directly to inflammation, angiogenesis, or neuronal regeneration.

Finally, OGN appears less directly relevant to stroke based on the provided annotation, which emphasizes bone formation in cooperation with TGF-beta signaling. Nevertheless, a limited mechanistic connection can be inferred because TGF-beta pathways are important regulators of extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis, inflammation, and vascular responses after stroke. If OGN participates more broadly in matrix-associated TGF-beta biology beyond skeletal tissues, it could potentially influence post-ischemic remodeling. However, from the information supplied here, the evidence for a meaningful stroke connection is comparatively weak, and OGN does not stand out as a primary candidate relative to TNC, CHI3L1, or IGFBP7.

### Pleural mesothelioma (WP:WP5087) 

Pleural mesothelioma is a malignant disease arising from mesothelial cells of the pleura and is biologically characterized by chronic inflammation, diffuse local invasion along the pleural surface, marked intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity, and recurrent alterations in tumor suppressor programs such as BRCA1 associated protein 1, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A, and neurofibromin 2. Contemporary clinical and molecular studies indicate that pleural mesothelioma is not a single uniform entity, but rather a spectrum of diseases defined by histologic subtype, immune microenvironment, genomic instability, epigenetic state, and tumor cell morphology. Multiomic analyses have shown that adaptive immune response, methylation state, ploidy, and morphology are major axes of biological variation, while spatial profiling has demonstrated substantial heterogeneity across different pleural sites, including variation in extracellular matrix programs, cell adhesion pathways, and immune contexture. Therapeutically, pleural mesothelioma has been managed with combinations of surgery, radiotherapy, platinum plus pemetrexed chemotherapy, immune checkpoint blockade, and emerging targeted or metabolic strategies, although outcomes remain poor overall. Radical surgical approaches such as extrapleural pneumonectomy or extended pleurectomy decortication can produce substantial perioperative morbidity, whereas systemic treatments including nivolumab plus ipilimumab, durvalumab with platinum and pemetrexed, pegargiminase with chemotherapy, and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 inhibition reflect the increasing importance of tumor immunology and molecular stratification in this disease. Thus, the pleural mesothelioma pathway is best understood as an integrated oncologic program involving inflammation, coagulation perturbation, immune remodeling, tissue invasion, and treatment related systemic stress.

Against this biological background, the possible relationship between pleural mesothelioma and stroke appears to be better explained by convergent clinical and systemic mechanisms than by a single shared canonical signaling pathway. The most direct evidence comes from a reported case in which pleural mesothelioma presented with acute ischemic stroke caused by internal carotid artery thrombotic occlusion; this patient showed thrombocytosis, hyperfibrinogenemia, and elevated C reactive protein, strongly suggesting that pleural mesothelioma can create a systemic prothrombotic and inflammatory state capable of precipitating large artery cerebral ischemia, and that restoration of carotid patency improved neurological outcome (PubMed:20036493). This observation is biologically plausible in light of broader mesothelioma literature describing the disease as an inflammation driven malignancy with substantial immune remodeling and extracellular matrix dysregulation, features that are also central to thrombosis, endothelial activation, and vascular injury. Multiomic and spatial studies further indicate that pleural mesothelioma exhibits marked heterogeneity in adaptive immune response and immune mediator expression, implying persistent systemic and local inflammatory signaling that could favor platelet activation and coagulation imbalance (PubMed:36928603, PubMed:34261524). In addition, several treatments used in pleural mesothelioma may modify stroke risk indirectly through cardiopulmonary toxicity, infection, or treatment related vascular complications. Major surgery for resectable disease is associated with high rates of serious adverse events, including cardiac and respiratory disorders and infections, all of which can amplify perioperative cerebrovascular risk in vulnerable patients (PubMed:33450184, PubMed:38740044). Systemic therapies also carry vascular relevance: pemetrexed based treatment has been noted to require monitoring for rare but severe adverse effects including stroke, while immune checkpoint blockade has produced severe immune related toxicities such as encephalitis and heart failure, which reflect the capacity of these regimens to induce systemic inflammatory injury with potential neurological consequences (PubMed:16400741, PubMed:33485464). Collectively, the available evidence suggests that pleural mesothelioma may be related to stroke primarily through cancer associated hypercoagulability, inflammation driven endothelial and platelet activation, and treatment associated systemic complications rather than through a stroke specific molecular pathway intrinsic to the tumor alone.[PubMed:20036493](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20036493) [PubMed:36928603](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36928603) [PubMed:34261524](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34261524) [PubMed:33450184](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33450184) [PubMed:38740044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38740044) [PubMed:16400741](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16400741) [PubMed:33485464](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33485464) 

Building on this disease level interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides a more focused view of how stroke associated biology may intersect with the pleural mesothelioma pathway.

There were 18 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing pleural mesothelioma as a malignant disease driven by chronic inflammation, diffuse pleural invasion, marked intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity, recurrent disruption of tumor suppressor programs including BRCA1 associated protein 1, cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A, and neurofibromin 2, and therapeutic exposure to surgery, radiotherapy, platinum plus pemetrexed chemotherapy, immune checkpoint blockade, pegargiminase, and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 inhibition; taken together, this enrichment pattern suggests that 18 of 18 analyzed proteins converge on a biologic program linking inflammation, coagulation disturbance, immune remodeling, tissue invasion, genomic instability, epigenetic variation, and treatment-related systemic stress in stroke.

To place these proteins into a network context, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for the 18 enriched proteins and provides direct access to the STRING webpage for additional inspection of network level evidence.

![PPI Network](imgs/d14fe01c-562f-40cb-b316-f366bd36e288.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=F453AA6C5CE9C44A)

With this network overview in mind, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several significant proteins that may help explain the observed intersection between pleural mesothelioma related biology and stroke associated processes. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

MDK is the most clearly stroke-relevant protein in this list because its annotated functions map directly onto several core mechanisms of ischemic and hemorrhagic brain injury. First, MDK is a potent regulator of inflammation: it promotes neutrophil and macrophage recruitment to sites of injury and can amplify chemokine expression, while also shaping adaptive immunity by suppressing tolerogenic dendritic cell development and promoting T-cell expansion and T helper 1 differentiation. These activities are highly pertinent to stroke, in which post-ischemic neuroinflammation contributes both to acute tissue damage and to later repair processes (PubMed:10683378, PubMed:22323540, PubMed:24458438). Second, MDK has strong prosurvival and regenerative properties. It activates anti-apoptotic mitogen activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling, promotes tissue regeneration after injury, and supports survival and growth of neural precursor cells and embryonic neurons, suggesting a plausible role in limiting neuronal death and supporting recovery after cerebral ischemia (PubMed:10772929, PubMed:12122009, PubMed:24458438). Third, MDK is relevant to post-stroke neurovascular remodeling because it enhances vascular endothelial proliferation, induces vascular endothelial growth factor A expression and nitric oxide synthase activity, and contributes to vasodilation and arteriogenesis, all of which are mechanistically linked to reperfusion, collateral circulation, and repair of the neurovascular unit. In addition, its ability to promote cell migration, epithelial to mesenchymal transition, and smooth muscle cell migration suggests a role in vascular remodeling after injury, which may be beneficial for recovery but could also contribute to pathological remodeling depending on context (PubMed:18469519). Finally, MDK directly participates in neuronal processes central to stroke recovery, including neuronal migration, neurite outgrowth, cell adhesion, and oligodendroglial precursor-like cell elongation, indicating potential involvement in axonal plasticity and remyelination during the subacute and chronic phases of stroke. Taken together, MDK appears to be a multifunctional mediator positioned at the intersection of neuroinflammation, neuronal survival, angiogenesis, and tissue repair, which may make it particularly relevant to stroke pathobiology and recovery.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

In comparison with MDK, the next candidate appears to connect to stroke more indirectly through vascular structure and contractile biology.

ACTA2 is potentially relevant to stroke because actin cytoskeletal dynamics are fundamental to vascular smooth muscle contraction, cell migration, and structural remodeling of the vessel wall. Although the provided annotation is general, ACTA2 is especially notable in the cerebrovascular context because smooth muscle cell contractility influences vascular tone, cerebral blood flow regulation, and the integrity of larger arteries and arterioles. These processes are directly relevant to stroke susceptibility and outcome, particularly in relation to vessel narrowing, hemodynamic instability, and post-injury vascular remodeling. However, compared with MDK, the stroke connection is less specifically supported by the supplied functional description, which only establishes a broad role in cell motility rather than explicitly linking ACTA2 to inflammation, neuronal survival, angiogenesis, or brain repair. Therefore, ACTA2 should be regarded as a plausible but less strongly prioritized stroke-related candidate based on the current annotation.

### external encapsulating structure (GO:0030312) 

The external encapsulating structure pathway refers to biological structures positioned outside the plasma membrane that surround the whole cell or multicellular unit. In human biology and disease, this concept includes extracellular coverings and externally organized structural layers that mediate mechanical protection, adhesion, signaling exchange, and interactions with the surrounding microenvironment. In the context of vascular and neurological disease, this pathway may be understood as encompassing extracellular structural components and cell-associated outer assemblies that shape how blood cells, platelets, endothelial cells, immune cells, and tissue elements interact outside the cell boundary. These structures include extracellular matrix-like scaffolds, platelet-rich outer thrombus layers, von Willebrand factor-rich networks, neutrophil extracellular traps, and membrane-derived extracellular vesicles that carry regulatory cargo between cells. Although extracellular vesicles are not static coverings in the classical sense, they are membrane-enclosed structures released from cells into the extracellular space and therefore may represent an important extension of cell exterior biology. Collectively, external encapsulating structures could influence thrombosis, fibrinolysis resistance, vascular remodeling, inflammation, endothelial communication, and tissue repair, all of which are central processes in stroke pathobiology.  

Building on this conceptual framework, the publications suggest that the relevance of the external encapsulating structure pathway to stroke may be most apparent in ischemic stroke, where extracellularly organized structures directly shape thrombus formation, persistence, and post-ischemic repair. A key observation is that acute ischemic stroke thrombi possess a highly organized outer shell composed predominantly of platelet-rich material surrounding the thrombus core, and this external shell contains extracellular elements such as von Willebrand factor multimers and neutrophil extracellular traps that promote resistance to tissue plasminogen activator-mediated fibrinolysis. This finding suggests that the behavior of the occlusive clot may depend not only on fibrin, but also on its outer structural architecture and associated extracellular network components (PubMed:35873787). In turn, this places external encapsulating structures near the center of treatment responsiveness, because the outer thrombus organization may act as a barrier to clot dissolution and thereby contribute to failed reperfusion or incomplete recanalization. Beyond the clot itself, extracellular vesicles represent another major manifestation of this pathway in stroke. Reviews of ischemic stroke biology indicate that extracellular vesicles transport noncoding regulatory ribonucleic acids between cells and modulate angiogenesis, vascular remodeling, and neurological recovery after cerebral ischemia, suggesting that extracellular membrane-bound particles function as intercellular carriers that reshape the post-stroke tissue environment (PubMed:36592424). This concept is further supported by clinical biomarker work showing that microvesicle-incorporated micro ribonucleic acids are altered in cancer-associated ischemic stroke and that one such extracellular vesicle cargo, micro ribonucleic acid two hundred five-five prime, can promote arterial thrombosis in vivo, thereby linking extracellular membrane structures to stroke-associated hypercoagulability and embolic risk (PubMed:37106564). A therapeutic extension of this biology is illustrated by biomimetic nanomedicine, in which macrophage membrane-camouflaged liposomes with a shell-core external structure improved targeting, reduced inflammation and apoptosis, and ameliorated neurological injury in experimental ischemic stroke, further supporting the possible importance of cell-exterior structural design in modulating stroke outcomes (PubMed:38474179). Taken together, the available evidence may support a coherent model in which external encapsulating structures contribute to stroke through three interconnected mechanisms: formation of a protective and fibrinolysis-resistant outer clot architecture, extracellular vesicle-mediated propagation of prothrombotic and reparative signals, and exploitable surface-based therapeutic targeting strategies for ischemic brain injury.[PubMed:35873787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35873787) [PubMed:36592424](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36592424) [PubMed:37106564](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37106564) [PubMed:38474179](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38474179) 

Consistent with this literature-based view, there were 33 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the external encapsulating structure pathway, a biological theme centered on structures positioned outside the plasma membrane that organize extracellular protection, adhesion, signaling exchange, thrombus architecture, inflammatory cell interaction, and tissue remodeling in stroke. This set of 33 proteins points to a quantitatively substantial extracellular component within stroke biology, in line with the contribution of cell-exterior structural organization to thrombosis, fibrinolysis resistance, endothelial dysfunction, immune activation, and post-injury repair. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 33 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network inspection and functional exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/787cae8d-7c7b-4319-8c0f-3b7dfb9f94fe.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=A7CB5CFD87C74D7B)

With this network-level context in place, the function enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help clarify how this extracellular theme relates to stroke biology. We introduce these proteins in detail below.  

ANGPT2 appears highly relevant to stroke because cerebrovascular disease is fundamentally shaped by endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier instability, inflammation, and post-ischemic vascular remodeling. The angiopoietin-TEK/TIE2 axis governs whether vessels remain quiescent and stable or become permissive to sprouting and remodeling. In the setting of stroke, these processes are central to both acute injury and recovery: impaired vascular stability can facilitate leakage of plasma proteins and leukocyte infiltration, thereby amplifying neuroinflammation and edema, whereas controlled angiogenesis may support tissue repair during the subacute phase. The description provided indicates that ANGPT2 modulates ANGPT1-TEK signaling, can compete for the same binding site, and influences phosphoinositide three-kinase-protein kinase B and focal adhesion kinase-extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathways, all of which are mechanistically linked to endothelial survival and barrier integrity. Thus, ANGPT2 stands out as a plausible mediator of ischemia-induced vascular destabilization as well as later-stage neovascular remodeling, two hallmark features of stroke pathobiology.  

Closely related to this vascular remodeling theme, EGFL7 is notable in stroke because it is a vascular developmental and remodeling factor with direct effects on endothelial organization and vessel formation. Following cerebral ischemia, restoration of microvascular integrity and re-establishment of perfusion are critical determinants of tissue salvage and neurological recovery. EGFL7-mediated vascular tubulogenesis and endothelial adhesion suggest a role in rebuilding damaged vascular networks after ischemic injury. Its inhibition of smooth muscle cell migration may also influence vascular wall remodeling and possibly limit maladaptive responses in injured vessels. Because stroke recovery depends in part on coordinated angiogenesis and stabilization of the neurovascular unit, EGFL7 is particularly relevant as a candidate regulator of post-stroke vascular repair.  

In a similar manner, IGFBP7 is of particular interest in stroke because its annotated functions converge on vascular homeostasis, endothelial biology, and angiogenesis. Prostacyclin production is especially relevant, as prostacyclin is vasoprotective, anti-platelet, and anti-inflammatory, all of which are highly pertinent to ischemic cerebrovascular injury. In addition, the recently described IGFBP7-CD93 interaction in angiogenesis suggests a role in endothelial remodeling and revascularization after injury. Since stroke outcome is strongly influenced by microvascular patency, endothelial activation, and the balance between thrombosis and repair, IGFBP7 emerges as a potentially meaningful mediator linking vascular signaling to both acute ischemic damage and subsequent recovery.[PubMed:38218180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38218180) 

Extending from vascular signaling to extracellular matrix regulation, TIMP1 is strongly connected to stroke because matrix metalloproteinases are central effectors of blood-brain barrier breakdown, extracellular matrix degradation, hemorrhagic transformation, and inflammatory tissue injury after cerebral ischemia. By inhibiting matrix metalloproteinase one, matrix metalloproteinase two, matrix metalloproteinase three, matrix metalloproteinase seven, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, matrix metalloproteinase ten, matrix metalloproteinase eleven, matrix metalloproteinase twelve, matrix metalloproteinase thirteen, and matrix metalloproteinase sixteen, TIMP1 may counteract proteolytic destruction of the vascular basement membrane and perivascular matrix. This is particularly important in acute stroke, where excessive matrix metalloproteinase activity contributes to edema and secondary injury. Its additional signaling roles through CD63 and integrin subunit beta one suggest that TIMP1 may also influence tissue remodeling and cell survival during recovery. Thus, TIMP1 stands out as a protein with direct mechanistic relevance to both acute neurovascular injury and later reparative remodeling.  

This matrix-centered perspective also helps place TNC in context. TNC is highly pertinent to stroke because it bridges two major dimensions of post-stroke biology: extracellular matrix remodeling and neural repair. Stroke induces profound restructuring of the peri-infarct matrix, and proteins that regulate cell migration, neurite extension, and synaptic plasticity can shape functional recovery. TNC also promotes endothelial migration and sprouting, implying a role in post-ischemic angiogenesis. This dual neurovascular relevance is especially important in stroke, where successful recovery requires coordinated vascular remodeling together with axonal sprouting and circuit reorganization. Therefore, TNC stands out as a plausible contributor to both injury-associated matrix changes and regenerative processes in the recovering brain.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

Moving from structural remodeling toward integrated inflammatory and reparative signaling, MDK is among the most compelling stroke-related proteins in this list because it connects inflammation, angiogenesis, neuronal survival, and tissue repair. These are all core mechanisms in ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. The provided annotation indicates that MDK recruits inflammatory cells, modulates dendritic cell and T-cell responses, promotes epithelial and neuronal survival, enhances angiogenesis, induces vascular endothelial growth factor A expression, and activates anti-apoptotic mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling. In the context of stroke, these activities could have both harmful and beneficial consequences depending on timing: early inflammatory recruitment may exacerbate injury, whereas later pro-survival and pro-angiogenic actions may support recovery and tissue remodeling. Its established roles in neurite outgrowth and neuronal migration further strengthen its relevance to neurorepair after stroke. Overall, MDK stands out as a multifunctional mediator acting at the interface of neuroinflammation, vascular remodeling, and regeneration.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Within this broader inflammatory framework, CHI3L1 is relevant to stroke primarily because it is a tissue remodeling and inflammatory mediator. Post-stroke injury is driven not only by ischemia itself but also by secondary immune activation, glial responses, and remodeling of damaged tissue. The annotation highlights roles in inflammatory cell regulation, macrophage polarization, apoptosis control, and protein kinase B one signaling, all of which are mechanistically plausible in the injured brain. Although the listed functions are not brain-specific, CHI3L1 stands out as a marker and potential mediator of sterile inflammation and repair responses, processes that are central to infarct evolution and recovery. Its involvement in shaping immune-cell behavior and tissue adaptation makes it a meaningful candidate in the broader inflammatory biology of stroke.  

A related but somewhat more immunoregulatory example is LGALS9, which is potentially important in stroke because it combines immunomodulatory and anti-angiogenic functions. Stroke pathology is profoundly influenced by innate and adaptive immune responses, including cytokine production and leukocyte recruitment, while later recovery depends partly on angiogenesis within peri-infarct tissue. A protein that suppresses interferon gamma production by natural killer cells may alter the inflammatory milieu after cerebral ischemia, and its anti-angiogenic activity could influence vascular remodeling during recovery. Although its direct role in stroke is less specific than some other proteins in this list, LGALS9 stands out as a plausible regulator of the balance between post-stroke inflammation and reparative neovascularization.  

Continuing with the theme of immune restraint, FGL1 is noteworthy in stroke because post-stroke immunoregulation is increasingly recognized as a major determinant of outcome. Through binding to lymphocyte activation gene three, FGL1 suppresses antigen-specific T-cell activation, indicating a potentially important role in adaptive immune restraint. In stroke, this may be relevant in at least two ways: limiting excessive neuroinflammation that worsens tissue damage, but also possibly contributing to the systemic immunosuppressive state that predisposes patients to infection. The explicit identification of FGL1 as a major ligand responsible for lymphocyte activation gene three inhibitory function makes it particularly interesting in relation to immune checkpoint biology in cerebrovascular disease.[PubMed:30580966](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30580966) 

Shifting from acute immune and vascular responses to upstream risk biology, ANGPTL4 is relevant to stroke because dyslipidemia is a major driver of atherosclerosis and ischemic cerebrovascular disease. By inhibiting lipoprotein lipase and controlling triglyceride clearance, ANGPTL4 influences circulating lipid handling, which can affect vascular risk over the long term. Although this function is less directly tied to acute stroke injury than endothelial or inflammatory mediators, it is highly pertinent to stroke susceptibility, especially in the context of large-artery atherosclerosis and cardiometabolic disease. Therefore, ANGPTL4 stands out as a protein more closely linked to stroke risk biology than to acute neurovascular damage.[PubMed:19270337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19270337) [PubMed:21398697](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21398697) [PubMed:27929370](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27929370) [PubMed:29899144](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899144) 

In parallel with these risk-related mechanisms, AMBP is potentially relevant to stroke because coagulation and thrombus formation are central to ischemic stroke pathogenesis. Its ability to inhibit factor ten a and interfere with prothrombin activation points to a direct connection with the coagulation cascade, raising the possibility that it could influence thrombosis risk or endogenous anticoagulant balance. Additionally, inhibition of mast cell proteases may affect vascular inflammation and permeability. Although the annotation does not directly establish a cerebrovascular role, the combination of anticoagulant and anti-protease functions makes AMBP mechanistically relevant to thromboinflammatory pathways involved in stroke.  

Another protein that may connect vascular risk with inflammatory injury is COLEC12. COLEC12 is of interest for stroke because it links vascular inflammation, innate immunity, and oxidized lipid handling. Recognition and uptake of oxidized low-density lipoprotein by endothelial cells is particularly relevant to atherosclerosis, a major cause of ischemic stroke. In addition, scavenger receptor-mediated endothelial responses can influence vascular inflammation and dysfunction, both of which contribute to plaque progression and cerebrovascular risk. Its possible role in amyloid beta clearance may also be relevant to cerebral small vessel disease and vascular cognitive impairment, which often overlap with stroke-related pathology. Thus, COLEC12 stands out mainly in relation to stroke risk mechanisms rooted in vascular injury and inflammation.  

Returning to reparative remodeling, SMOC2 is relevant to stroke because extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenesis are essential components of post-ischemic repair. By promoting endothelial proliferation and migration, SMOC2 may support revascularization of injured tissue, while its matrix-assembly function suggests a role in rebuilding the structural microenvironment of the neurovascular unit. These properties are particularly important during the subacute and chronic phases of stroke recovery, when restoration of vascular support can facilitate neuronal survival and plasticity. Accordingly, SMOC2 stands out as a plausible contributor to regenerative vascular remodeling after stroke.  

Alongside these reparative processes, SPON2 may be relevant to stroke through its role in innate immunity and extracellular matrix-associated inflammatory signaling. Neuroinflammation after stroke involves activation of macrophages and other innate immune pathways, and extracellular matrix-associated pattern-recognition molecules can shape these responses. Although SPON2 is more directly linked to antimicrobial defense than to cerebrovascular biology per se, its ability to regulate macrophage phagocytosis and inflammatory initiation suggests that it could influence post-stroke immune activation and tissue clearance. It is therefore a secondary but still potentially meaningful candidate in the inflammatory dimension of stroke.  

Finally, CCN3 is relevant to stroke because it intersects with angiogenesis, developmental signaling, and cellular differentiation. Its negative regulation of endothelial proliferation and sprouting suggests that it may restrain vascular remodeling after ischemic injury. In the brain, where repair requires a tightly controlled balance between angiogenesis and tissue organization, such inhibitory signaling may influence recovery trajectories. In addition, its broader effects on differentiation and hypoxia inducible factor one subunit alpha-related signaling imply possible relevance to hypoxic adaptation. Thus, CCN3 stands out as a regulator that may modulate the reparative angiogenic response after stroke.

### Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (KEGG:04060) 

The cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway is a core intercellular communication network that governs how immune, vascular, glial, and neural cells exchange inflammatory, reparative, and homeostatic signals. It comprises soluble ligands such as interleukins, chemokines, interferons, tumor necrosis factor family members, colony-stimulating factors, and growth factors, together with their cognate membrane receptors. Through ligand-receptor binding, this pathway initiates downstream signaling programs that regulate leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, blood-brain barrier integrity, microglial and macrophage polarization, neuronal survival or death, angiogenesis, thromboinflammation, and tissue remodeling. In the setting of cerebral ischemia, cytokine-receptor signaling is rapidly induced both within the ischemic brain and in the peripheral immune compartment. This pathway is therefore not a single linear cascade, but rather a signaling interface that integrates multiple biological processes central to stroke pathogenesis, including sterile inflammation, innate and adaptive immune activation, chemotaxis, vascular dysfunction, and post-ischemic repair. The publications provided consistently identify this pathway as one of the most significantly enriched pathways in ischemic stroke transcriptomic, epigenetic, non-coding ribonucleic acid, and single-cell analyses, indicating that dysregulated cytokine-receptor communication is a recurrent systems-level feature of stroke biology.  

Building on this general framework, the studies provided further suggest that the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway may represent a recurrent molecular signature linking ischemic stroke to inflammatory injury, immune cell recruitment, neurovascular dysfunction, and subsequent repair. Multiple blood-based and tissue-level transcriptomic analyses identified this pathway among the most significantly enriched pathways in ischemic stroke, often alongside tumor necrosis factor signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, transforming growth factor beta signaling, and chemokine signaling, which together suggest that stroke induces a broad inflammatory communication program rather than isolated gene changes. Mechanistically, the pathway appears to contribute to stroke through several interconnected processes. First, it may amplify acute inflammation: key mediators such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 6, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8, and C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 were repeatedly implicated as hub or differentially expressed genes, and experimental inhibition of C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 reduced infarct size, neurological impairment, and expression of related inflammatory proteins, supporting a possible causal contribution of chemokine-driven injury. Second, it appears to shape immune cell behavior and cellular cross-talk: single-cell analysis showed enrichment of lactylation-related programs in natural killer cells and T cells, with predicted signaling to neural cells through tumor necrosis factor family ligand-receptor pairs, while other studies linked the pathway to immune infiltration patterns, microglial polarization, and sex-specific immune responses. Third, it may also be connected to vascular adaptation and repair, because angiogenesis-focused transcriptomic work in cerebral ischemia identified this pathway within competing endogenous ribonucleic acid networks that may regulate post-ischemic neovascularization. Fourth, the pathway appears to be embedded in higher-order regulatory layers, including circular ribonucleic acids, micro ribonucleic acids, messenger ribonucleic acid methylation, and methyltransferase-dependent methylation control, all of which converged on cytokine-receptor signaling as a major enriched process in stroke. Finally, several integrative network studies proposed therapeutically relevant nodes within this pathway, including tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 6, vascular endothelial growth factor A, angiotensin receptor type 1, interleukin 7 receptor, and C-C chemokine receptor type 7, suggesting that modulation of cytokine-receptor communication may have diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic value. Taken together, the available evidence suggests that the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway may be centrally involved in the initiation and propagation of post-ischemic inflammation, the recruitment and activation of peripheral and resident immune cells, the regulation of neurovascular injury, and the orchestration of endogenous recovery responses in stroke.[PubMed:41724973](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41724973) [PubMed:35419038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35419038) [PubMed:36225588](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36225588) [PubMed:41456745](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41456745) [PubMed:38052584](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38052584) [PubMed:40540134](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40540134) [PubMed:37600392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37600392) [PubMed:40127530](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40127530) [PubMed:32164735](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32164735) [PubMed:32422289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32422289) [PubMed:33818699](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33818699) [PubMed:36279101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36279101) [PubMed:38135832](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38135832) [PubMed:40464505](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40464505) [PubMed:31899762](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31899762) [PubMed:41291461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41291461) 

To connect these pathway-level observations with the present enrichment results, it is useful to consider the number of stroke-associated proteins mapped to this pathway. There were 29 stroke-associated proteins significantly enriched in the cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction pathway, a central intercellular signaling system that coordinates inflammatory, vascular, glial, and neuronal communication during cerebral ischemia. This enrichment supports a quantitatively substantial involvement of cytokine-mediated ligand-receptor signaling in stroke biology, with the 29 proteins collectively mapping to a pathway that regulates leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, blood-brain barrier stability, microglial and macrophage functional polarization, neuronal injury responses, angiogenesis, thromboinflammation, and tissue remodeling. In the context of stroke, the concentration of 29 disease-associated proteins within this pathway suggests that dysregulated extracellular signaling may represent not a peripheral feature, but rather a core systems-level component of ischemic pathogenesis and post-ischemic repair.

To further illustrate how these 29 proteins may relate to one another, the network view below provides a protein-protein interaction overview. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 29 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/6780ecd3-0fe3-4acf-8e06-169f2619a8d3.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=6F54E328C3E365C9)

With this network context in place, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

CCL14 stands out as potentially relevant to stroke because post-stroke injury is strongly shaped by chemokine gradients that govern leukocyte trafficking across the neurovascular unit. This receptor is unusual in that it does not primarily signal in the canonical chemokine-receptor manner; instead, it controls chemokine bioavailability by scavenging inflammatory chemokines and by supporting endothelial transcytosis and erythrocyte buffering of circulating chemokines. These properties are highly pertinent to ischemic stroke, where excessive recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes amplifies blood-brain barrier disruption, edema, and secondary tissue injury. By influencing the local and systemic availability of inflammatory chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 2, C-C motif chemokine ligand 5, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8, and related ligands, CCL14 may shape both the intensity and spatial distribution of post-ischemic inflammation. Its endothelial role is particularly notable because endothelial chemokine presentation is a key step in leukocyte adhesion and transmigration, processes central to reperfusion injury and infarct evolution.  

Closely related to this theme of chemokine-directed immune cell trafficking, CCL15 also appears potentially relevant in stroke. CCL15 is among the most compelling stroke-related candidates in this list because its annotated functions directly intersect with core mechanisms of ischemic brain injury: leukocyte recruitment, amplification of inflammation, and neuroinflammatory signaling. The protein contributes to the migration of monocytes, macrophages, T cells, dendritic cells, and neutrophils, all of which are major participants in post-stroke sterile inflammation. Particularly relevant is the reported mediation of neutrophil migration after C-C motif chemokine ligand 3 stimulation, accompanied by sequential tumor necrosis factor alpha and leukotriene B4 release, since these mediators are strongly implicated in endothelial activation, blood-brain barrier damage, and infarct expansion. The note that activation by C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 can drive neuroinflammation through extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1 and extracellular signal-regulated kinase 2 signaling further strengthens its relevance, as C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 and extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway activation have both been linked to secondary neuronal injury after stroke. In addition, monocyte migration in response to C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 4 suggests a possible contribution to thrombo-inflammatory processes, which are central to ischemic stroke pathophysiology and vascular remodeling after injury.[PubMed:14991608](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14991608) [PubMed:15905581](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15905581) [PubMed:29930254](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29930254) 

Moving from chemokine biology to broader stress and inflammatory signaling, EDA2R may represent a more indirect but still potentially informative candidate. EDA2R is potentially relevant to stroke because it couples extracellular cues to nuclear factor kappa B and c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, two pathways that are central to ischemia-induced inflammation, stress responses, and cell death. Although its best-characterized biology is not stroke-specific, activation of tumor necrosis factor receptor associated factor-dependent nuclear factor kappa B and c-Jun N-terminal kinase cascades could plausibly influence endothelial activation, glial inflammatory responses, and neuronal injury in the ischemic brain. These signaling modules are repeatedly implicated in post-stroke cytokine production, apoptosis-related signaling, and secondary tissue damage. Therefore, EDA2R may be of interest as an upstream modulator of inflammatory and stress signaling, even if the present annotation provides less direct evidence for stroke involvement than the chemokine- or cytokine-related proteins in this dataset.  

In contrast to proteins that may amplify inflammatory injury, IL10RB appears more closely aligned with counter-regulatory immune signaling. IL10RB is highly relevant to stroke because it sits at the intersection of anti-inflammatory and innate immune signaling. Its role as an essential receptor component for interleukin 10 is particularly important, as interleukin 10 is a major immunoregulatory cytokine that can suppress excessive inflammatory activation after cerebral ischemia. In the context of stroke, controlled IL10RB-mediated signaling may help limit damaging cytokine production, leukocyte-mediated injury, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction. In parallel, its participation in type three interferon signaling through Janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription and induction of interferon-stimulated genes suggests a broader role in post-stroke immune regulation, which is clinically relevant because stroke patients often develop systemic immune dysregulation and heightened susceptibility to infection. Thus, IL10RB may influence both neuroinflammatory injury within the brain and peripheral host defense after stroke, making it a particularly notable protein in this list.  

Shifting from immune regulation toward neuronal survival and repair, INHBB may be relevant in a different, more indirect manner. INHBB is of potential interest in stroke primarily because activin-related signaling has recognized links to tissue repair, inflammation, and neuronal survival. The annotation specifically mentions nerve cell survival, which makes this protein biologically relevant to ischemic brain injury, where neuronal death and attempted recovery are central outcomes. In addition, the broader roles of inhibin and activin family members in endocrine and metabolic regulation may be indirectly important, since metabolic state, insulin signaling, and systemic stress responses influence stroke risk and recovery. However, compared with the immune receptors and tumor necrosis factor family proteins in this dataset, the functional connection of INHBB to stroke is more indirect and likely relates to neuroprotection, repair, or systemic homeostatic responses rather than acute leukocyte-driven injury.  

Returning to stress-associated injury pathways, RELT may also warrant consideration. RELT is potentially relevant to stroke because apoptosis and stress-activated mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling are major determinants of secondary neuronal and glial injury after ischemia. The reported ability of RELT to activate p38 and c-Jun N-terminal kinase is noteworthy, as both pathways are strongly associated with inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and ischemia-induced cell death. The explicit suggestion that RELT may participate in apoptosis further supports a plausible role in infarct progression. Although the current annotation does not directly tie RELT to cerebrovascular disease, proteins that converge on p38, c-Jun N-terminal kinase, and apoptotic mechanisms are often mechanistically relevant in stroke, particularly during the subacute phase when programmed cell death and inflammatory amplification continue after the initial ischemic insult.[PubMed:19969290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19969290) [PubMed:28688764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28688764) [PubMed:16530727](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16530727) [PubMed:30506946](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30506946) 

A related extension of this theme is seen in tumor necrosis factor receptor family members that may couple inflammatory signaling to cell death programs. TNFRSF19 is relevant to stroke because it links tumor necrosis factor receptor biology to two central features of ischemic injury: inflammatory transcriptional activation and cell death. Activation of c-Jun and nuclear factor kappa B suggests the capacity to regulate stress-responsive and pro-inflammatory gene programs in neurons, glia, or vascular cells after ischemia. Its reported ability to promote caspase-independent cell death is also notable, as stroke pathology includes multiple non-apoptotic and caspase-independent death pathways in addition to classical apoptosis. The possibility that alternative isoforms act as decoy receptors introduces an additional layer of complexity, raising the prospect that TNFRSF19 could either exacerbate or buffer injury depending on isoform expression and tissue context. This makes it a plausible modulator of post-stroke inflammatory and degenerative signaling.  

Another tumor necrosis factor receptor family member with potentially broad relevance is TNFRSF6B. TNFRSF6B is particularly interesting in stroke because its annotated functions map onto several pathophysiological domains relevant to both acute injury and recovery. Nuclear factor kappa B activation may contribute to inflammatory amplification after ischemia, while promotion of caspase activation and apoptosis suggests a potential role in cell loss within ischemic tissue. Equally important is its inhibitory effect on vascular endothelial growth and angiogenesis in vitro. Angiogenesis is a key component of post-stroke repair and neurovascular remodeling, especially during recovery phases; therefore, a factor that suppresses endothelial growth could adversely affect tissue revascularization and functional recovery. Its effect on splenocyte alloactivation also points to broader immune-regulatory capacity, which is relevant because splenic and systemic immune responses substantially influence stroke outcomes.  

Finally, extending from innate and vascular signaling to adaptive immunity, TNFRSF9 may provide insight into later immune-mediated phases of stroke pathology. TNFRSF9 is relevant to stroke because it regulates T-cell activation and survival, processes increasingly recognized as important in post-stroke neuroinflammation. Although its canonical function is described in antiviral and antitumor immunity, enhancement of cluster of differentiation 8-positive T-cell survival and cytotoxicity may have implications for delayed immune-mediated tissue injury after cerebral ischemia. Cytotoxic lymphocytes can contribute to secondary neuronal damage and prolonged inflammatory remodeling in the injured brain. At the same time, because stroke also induces systemic immunosuppression, TNFRSF9-related pathways may affect the balance between harmful neuroinflammation and protective host defense. Thus, TNFRSF9 is mechanistically important as a marker of adaptive immune activation that could modulate stroke outcome depending on timing and immune context.
